content: The longissimus muscle is located lateral to the semispinalis muscle. It is the longest portion of the sacrospinalis muscle group and extends forward to attach to the transverse processes of the posterior cervical vertebrae. Longissimus dorsi The longissimus dorsi is the intermediate and largest segment of the sacrospinalis muscle group. In the lumbar region, it is blended with the iliocostalis lumborum. Some of its fibers attach along the entire length of the posterior surfaces of the transverse processes and the accessory processes of the lumbar vertebrae, as well as to the anterior layer of the lumbodorsal fascia. In the thoracic region, the muscle attaches via rounded tendons to the tips of the transverse processes of all thoracic vertebrae. Additionally, fleshy processes of the muscle insert into the lower nine or ten ribs, specifically between their tubercles and angles. Longissimus cervicis The longissimus cervicis, also known as the transversalis cervicis, is positioned medial to the longissimus dorsi. It originates via long, thin tendons from the summits of the transverse processes of the upper four or five thoracic vertebrae. It inserts via similar tendons into the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, spanning from the second to the sixth cervical vertebrae. Longissimus capitis The longissimus capitis, also referred to as the trachelomastoid muscle, is located medial to the longissimus cervicis, lying between it and the semispinalis capitis. It originates via tendons from the transverse processes of the upper four or five thoracic vertebrae and the articular processes of the lower three or four cervical vertebrae. The muscle inserts into the posterior margin of the mastoid process, beneath the splenius capitis and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Near its insertion, the muscle is almost always crossed by a tendinous intersection.
